questions.question: When should you panic vs return an error in Go?
questions.title: N Should You Panic Vs Return An
questions.direct_answer: Return an error for anything a caller could reasonably handle: missing file, bad input, failed network call. Panic for programmer bugs — an impossible state, a broken invariant, arithmetic you proved safe. Libraries should almost never panic on user input.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[panic] --> U1[deferred fn 1 runs — LIFO]
    U1 --> U2[deferred fn 0 runs]
    U2 -->|recover called| STOP[unwind stops → returns normally]
    U2 -->|no recover| EXIT[program exits + stack dump]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two mechanisms are built differently, which explains the rule.

An error value is just data: a struct or a string implementing `error`. It flows through return values like any other data, gets checked explicitly, and can carry context by wrapping. Nothing about an error is special to the runtime — it's ordinary Go.

A panic changes control flow. The moment `panic` executes, the current goroutine starts unwinding: each function's deferred calls run, in reverse order, until something calls `recover` or the program dies. That's a heavyweight, non-local jump — and it's exactly what makes it wrong for expected failures. If a missing file unwound your stack, every caller would need a recover block around every file operation — which is just exceptions with extra steps.

So the runtime gives errors the cheap, local, explicit path, and panics the expensive, non-local path. The cost difference is the design signal: use the cheap one for the common case. A library wrapping its panics with a deferred recover at its API boundary is converting 'programmer bug' into 'caller-visible error' — the right direction at the boundary.

questions.question: What happens when a panic occurs?
questions.title: Ppens When A Panic Occurs
questions.direct_answer: The goroutine unwinds: deferred functions run in LIFO order, then if nothing recovers, the program prints the panic value and stack trace and exits.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The unwinding order is what makes defer/recover work at all. Consider the pattern:



When doWork panics, the deferred closure runs first — because it was deferred in this function — and recover grabs the panic value before the unwind escapes. If the defer were placed AFTER doWork, the panic would pass the function before the closure was registered: recover has to be set up before the dangerous call, which is why defer sits at the top of the function.

The stack trace the runtime prints is the unwind path — the panic site plus every frame it passed through. That's why panics are diagnostic gold when they're genuine bugs: the trace tells you exactly which impossible state occurred and where.

questions.question: What is recover and where is it valid?
questions.title: Recover And Where Is It Valid
questions.direct_answer: recover() returns the panic value and stops the unwinding — but only inside a deferred function while a panic is in flight. Anywhere else it returns nil.

questions.question: Does panic in one goroutine crash the whole program?
questions.title: Does Panic In One Goroutine Crash The
questions.direct_answer: Yes. An unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the entire process — all goroutines die together. Each goroutine needs its own recover at its own boundary.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G1[G1] --> P1[P local queue]
    G2[G2] --> P1
    P1 --> M1[M runs Go code]
    P2[P] -.steal.-> P1
    M2[M in syscall] -.P handed off.-> M3[M takes over P]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Mechanically, each goroutine has its own stack and unwind is per-stack. When goroutine B panics, the runtime unwinds B's stack; when it runs out without finding a recover, there is nothing else to do safely — the other goroutines are in arbitrary states, possibly holding locks mid-operation, and the runtime has no safe way to pause and clean them. Exit is the only honest option.

That's the deep reason the goroutine-recover pattern exists: the only code that can catch a goroutine's panic is code inside that goroutine. Libraries like net/http actually do this for you in the request handler — http.Handler panics are recovered per-connection and turned into a closed connection — which is why a nil-map write in one HTTP handler doesn't kill your whole web server. Know where your runtime draws that boundary for you and where you must draw it yourself.

questions.question: Is panic/recover Go's exception handling?
questions.title: Is Panic/recover Go's Exception Handling
questions.direct_answer: No. Errors are values, returned and checked explicitly. Panic/recover is a crash mechanism with a recovery hatch for boundaries. Using panic for control flow defeats Go's explicit error design.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[panic] --> U1[deferred fn 1 runs — LIFO]
    U1 --> U2[deferred fn 0 runs]
    U2 -->|recover called| STOP[unwind stops → returns normally]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The design difference shows up in what each mechanism costs the reader. With exceptions, any call might throw anything — safety requires knowing the exception hierarchy, and the failure path is invisible at the call site. With Go errors, the failure path is the part after the `if` — you can read a function and see exactly which calls can fail and what happens then.

That's also why recover-as-control-flow is an anti-pattern: it reinstates the invisible control flow Go was designed to avoid, but with worse ergonomics than exceptions (no type-based dispatch, one-shot recover, defer-only placement). The Go standard library's own usage is the calibration: panics in the runtime for genuine invariant violations (nil map write, index out of range), errors for everything a caller could face, recover only at package boundaries like http's per-connection handler. When the standard library uses a mechanism sparingly, that's the target.
